title: Mock 5 · Rules & Revision
blurb: Mixed revision: regulatory limits, arbitrage, put-call parity, STT and settlement obligations.

questions.q: The SEBI group set up in June 1998 under Prof. J. R. Varma was asked to recommend:
options: Measures for risk containment in the derivatives market
questions.explanation: The J.R. Varma group recommended risk-containment measures: the margining system, initial margin methodology, net worth criteria, deposit requirements and real-time position monitoring.
hints: Taxation was not its brief.
Correct: risk containment in derivatives.
Not related.
Not related.

questions.q: Losses arising from fraud, inadequate documentation or improper execution of trades are examples of:
questions.explanation: The workbook lists operational risk as fraud, inadequate documentation, improper execution and similar failures.
hints: Price risk is loss due to adverse price moves.
Liquidity risk is the inability to exit a position.
Correct: operational risk.
Counterparty risk is default by the other party.

questions.q: As per SEBI's October 2025 prudential norms for derivatives on existing non-benchmark indices, the index must have a minimum of how many constituents?
questions.explanation: The norms require at least 14 constituents, a top constituent weight of at most 20%, a combined top-3 weight of at most 45%, and a descending weight structure.
hints: Too few.
20 is the maximum weight (%) of the top constituent, not the count.
Too many.
Correct: 14 constituents.

questions.q: Under SEBI's revised norms (effective November 2024), the lot size of index derivatives is fixed so that the contract value on the day of review lies between:
questions.explanation: A derivative contract must be worth at least ₹15 lakh at introduction, and the lot size is set so that its value on review day is within ₹15–20 lakh. The old ₹5–10 lakh band dated from 2015.
hints: Correct: ₹15–20 lakh.
That was the old range set in 2015.
Not the prescribed range.
Not the prescribed range.

questions.q: An arbitrageur buys a stock at ₹100 in the cash market and sells its futures at ₹110 (lot size 50). On expiry the stock closes at ₹95. Ignoring costs, what is the total profit for the lot?
questions.explanation: Cash leg: 95 − 100 = −5. Futures leg: 110 − 95 = +15. Net = +10 per share × 50 = ₹500. The ₹10 spread is locked in regardless of the expiry price.
hints: This counts only the cash loss.
Correct: locked spread of 10 × 50 = ₹500.
This counts only the futures gain.
The arbitrage is hedged and cannot lose here.

questions.q: An investor expects to receive a large sum next month to invest in equities and fears the market will rise before then. The appropriate futures hedge is to:
questions.explanation: This is a long hedge: going long index futures now means a market rise produces futures profits that offset the higher cost of buying shares later.
hints: A short hedge protects existing holdings against a fall.
Selling calls does not protect against a rally.
Correct: long hedge with index futures.
Puts protect against falls, not rises.

questions.q: Monthly Nifty, Bank Nifty and stock futures contracts listed on NSE expire on the:
options: Last Tuesday of the expiry month
Last Thursday of the expiry month
Last Wednesday of the expiry month
Last Friday of the expiry month
questions.explanation: NSE chose Tuesday as its expiry day, so monthly contracts expire on the last Tuesday (or the previous trading day if that is a holiday). BSE chose Thursday.
hints: Correct: last Tuesday.
Thursday is BSE's chosen expiry day.
Exchanges may choose only Tuesday or Thursday.
Exchanges may choose only Tuesday or Thursday.

questions.q: A stock trades at ₹500 while its one-month futures trades at ₹485, well below fair value. Ignoring costs, which arbitrage is appropriate?
options: Buy the stock and sell futures
Buy both the stock and futures
Sell the stock (or borrow and sell it) and buy futures
questions.explanation: Futures below fair value call for reverse cash-and-carry: short in the cash market and long in futures. The arbitrageur earns the gap plus interest on the sale proceeds.
hints: That is cash-and-carry, used when futures are OVERpriced.
Not an arbitrage; it doubles the exposure.
A naked short is not arbitrage.
Correct: reverse cash-and-carry.

questions.q: A stock trades at ₹1,240. The 1,300-strike put is quoted at ₹75. What is the time value of the put?
questions.explanation: Intrinsic value = 1,300 − 1,240 = 60. Time value = 75 − 60 = ₹15.
hints: That is the whole premium.
That is the intrinsic value.
You added intrinsic value to the premium.

questions.q: You sell a 2,000-strike put at ₹60 (lot size 250). The stock settles at ₹1,910 on expiry. What is your net P&L?
questions.explanation: Short put P&L per share = premium − (X − S) = 60 − 90 = −30. × 250 = −₹7,500.
hints: That is just the premium received.
This ignores the premium received.
The sign is wrong: the put finished deep enough in the money to cause a loss.

questions.q: How does a trader close out an existing long call position?
options: By buying a put with the same strike
By selling a call with the same strike price and expiry date
By buying another call of a higher strike
By selling futures on the same stock
questions.explanation: A closing transaction must be in an option with the same contract specifications. A long call is closed by a 'closing sale' of the same call (same strike and expiry). Buying a put does not close it.
hints: The workbook explicitly says buying a put does not close a long call.
Correct: closing sale of the identical option.
This creates a new position.
This hedges but does not close the option.

questions.q: For the buyer of an option (call or put), theta is usually:
questions.explanation: Options lose time value each day, so theta is usually negative for a long option, whether call or put.
hints: Positive theta benefits option writers, not buyers.
Time decay is not zero before expiry.
Theta and delta measure different things.
Correct: negative for long options.

questions.q: You buy one lot (75) of a Nifty 24,500 call at ₹120. Nifty settles at 24,800 on expiry. What is your net profit?
hints: This ignores the premium paid.
This is only the premium outlay.
This adds the premium instead of subtracting it.

questions.q: An investor holds a stock, sells an OTM call and buys an OTM put on it. This combined position is called a:
questions.explanation: A collar extends a covered call by adding a long OTM put. It puts a floor under the downside but reduces the maximum profit.
hints: A butterfly uses three strikes of the same option type (or a combination) without stock.
A strangle has no stock leg and buys both options.
A bull spread uses two options of the same type.
Correct: long stock + short call + long put = collar.

questions.q: A trader buys a 1,000-strike call at ₹40 and sells a 1,050-strike call at ₹18. What is the maximum profit of this spread?
questions.explanation: Bull call spread: net debit = 40 − 18 = 22. Maximum profit = (1,050 − 1,000) − 22 = ₹28. Maximum loss = ₹22 and BEP = 1,022.
hints: ₹22 is the maximum loss (net debit).
This ignores the premium paid.
That is just the short call premium.

questions.q: A stock trades at ₹1,000. A 3-month European call with a strike of ₹1,000 costs ₹50 and the interest rate is 6% p.a. (continuous). Using put-call parity, the fair price of the 1,000-strike put is about:
hints: Equal to the call only if interest is zero.
The interest effect was added instead of subtracted.
This subtracts the full call premium wrongly.

questions.q: A trader sells one lot (75) of an index option at a premium of ₹200. As per the workbook rates, the STT payable on this sale is:
questions.explanation: Premium value = 200 × 75 = ₹15,000. STT on the sale of an option = 0.15% of premium = ₹22.50, payable by the seller.
hints: This applies the 0.05% futures rate.
This uses 0.1%.
A decimal place is wrong.

questions.q: An exchange may introduce derivatives on an index only if constituents individually eligible for derivatives make up at least ___ of the index weight, and no single ineligible stock exceeds ___.
questions.explanation: At least 80% of the index weight must be in derivative-eligible stocks, and no single ineligible stock may have a weight above 5%.
hints: Both figures are wrong.
The eligible-weight figure is wrong.
Correct: 80% and 5%.
Both figures are wrong.

questions.q: When a trading member's systems are disrupted and the Investor Risk Reduction Access (IRRA) platform is enabled, investors can use it to:
options: Square off open positions and cancel pending orders only
Transfer their account to another broker
questions.explanation: IRRA lets investors close positions and cancel pending orders. It does not permit any action that increases risk, and it does not serve algo or institutional clients.
hints: Correct: risk-reducing actions only.
IRRA does not allow new positions.
Broker transfer is not an IRRA function.
IRRA excludes algorithmic trading.

questions.q: A client is short 2 lots (lot size 600) of a stock futures contract brought forward from yesterday. Yesterday's settlement price was ₹520 and today's is ₹532. Today's MTM is:
questions.explanation: For brought-forward positions, MTM = today's SP − previous SP = +12. A short loses when the price rises: −12 × 600 × 2 = −₹14,400, a debit.
hints: A short gains only when the price falls.
This counts only 1 lot.
Wrong sign and only 1 lot.

questions.q: On expiry, a client holds one lot (700 shares) of a long put on a stock with a strike of ₹900. The stock closes at ₹860. What is the settlement?
questions.explanation: Stock options are physically settled at the strike price. An exercised long put becomes a sell obligation: deliver 700 shares and receive 900 × 700 = ₹6,30,000 on T+1.
hints: Cash settlement applies to index options.
Correct: deliver shares, receive strike × lot.
The settlement value is at the strike price, not the market price.
That is the obligation of a short put that is assigned.

questions.q: The trading member-wise position limit in equity index option contracts is the higher of:
options: ₹7,500 crore or 15% of the total OI in index options
questions.explanation: For TMs, index futures and index options limits are each the higher of ₹7,500 crore or 15% of total OI in that product, applied per underlying index.
hints: ₹500 crore figures relate to index futures limits by client category.
Not the TM limit.
Correct: higher of ₹7,500 crore or 15% of OI.
₹10,000 crore is the PAN-level gross FutEq limit.

questions.q: Trading members must maintain trade confirmation slips and exercise notices from the trading system for a period of:
questions.explanation: Trade confirmation slips and exercise notices must be kept for 5 years.
hints: Too short.
8 years is the tax loss carry-forward period.
Too long.
Correct: 5 years.

questions.q: Under the presumptive taxation scheme of Section 44AD, F&O income is assessed at what rate of turnover, and up to what turnover limit?
questions.explanation: Section 44AD applies if total turnover does not exceed ₹2 crore. Gains are assessed at 6% of turnover, with no deductions for expenses.
hints: The rate is wrong.
₹10 crore is the turnover above which a tax audit is mandatory.
Correct: 6% of turnover, up to ₹2 crore.
Both figures are wrong.

questions.q: On the SMART ODR portal, once a dispute is referred to an ODR institution, the appointed conciliator should try to reach an amicable resolution within:
questions.explanation: The ODR institution appoints a sole independent conciliator to resolve the matter within 21 calendar days. If that fails, the investor may pursue online arbitration.
hints: 7 days is the window to signal an intention to challenge an award.
15 days is the deadline to pay an arbitral award.
Correct: 21 calendar days.
Too long.
